title: President Marcos, Chinese foreign minister discuss West Philippine Sea issues
summary: President Marcos is hopeful for “better” and “improved” relations with China, following his recent conversation with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Shenzhen, China.

blocks.text: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. arrives in a vehicle at the Philippine International Convention Center for the opening ceremonies of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Meetings in Manila on November 15, 2026.
MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos is hopeful for “better” and “improved” relations with China, following his recent conversation with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Shenzhen, China.
Marcos said while he didn’t get the chance to speak with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he had a “long conversation” with Wang on several matters, including the West Philippine Sea.

“As you can imagine, it’s very difficult to have any kind of extended interaction with President Xi, because he’s also very, very busy,” the President told the Philippine media delegation who covered his participation in the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ meeting and related activities yesterday.

“I had an opportunity during the gala dinner, quite by coincidence, or maybe by design, I don’t know, to sit next to Foreign Minister Wang Yi. And over dinner we had a long conversation on several matters,” he said.
According to Marcos, he discussed with Wang “how we can move together, how we can lower tensions in the West Philippine Sea, how we can deal with each other in a better way.”
Marcos said he is “very optimistic” that the Philippines and China will “find better ways to deal with the difficulties that we have.”

“I think, because Foreign Minister Wang Yi and I were able to speak, even though I wasn’t able to talk to President Xi, we were able to discuss a lot of things that I think will be for the better,” he said, emphasizing the two countries’ trade and investment relations.
Meanwhile, Marcos said China and all member-states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations are supportive of finalizing a code of conduct (COC) in the South China Sea.
“All the ASEAN leadership would like a COC. And I think, I feel it very strongly that China would also like to have a COC. And they say so,” Marcos said.
He credited the support and cooperation of the Chinese on the progress of finalizing the COC.

Marcos said Singapore, the next chair of the ASEAN, now holds the initiative to move things forward for the finalization of the COC, which seeks to establish rules for managing maritime disputes and preventing confrontations in the South China Sea.
“I’m highly encouraged by the attitude that they bring to those negotiations. And let’s really hope that Singapore will be able to host the actual finalization of the COC,” Marcos said.
At a press conference after the closing ceremony of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Pasay City on Tuesday, Marcos said the major issues surrounding the proposed rules have been settled.
